Abstract—Burnout is classified by the World Health Organization as an occupational phenomenon rather than a medical condition, a distinction that constrains what an automated system may legitimately claim. Detection in practice rests on periodic self-report inventories, administered infrequently, vulnerable to response bias, and silent on why a score was produced. Neural classifiers widen coverage but substitute one form of opacity for another. This paper presents a burnout detection system that separates measurement from explanation and enforces that separation architecturally. A four-stage pipeline scores workplace communication using a transformer sentiment classifier, a word-emotion lexicon and surface behavioural features, combined by a transparent additive rule in which every point is attributable to a named signal by construction. A retrieval-augmented language model then explains those scores and returns the specific records supporting each statement, so that a reader can check the reasoning rather than trust it. The two stages communicate through a single read-only file, which keeps the scoring stage authoritative and leaves the language model no means of altering a risk band. The implementation is verified by 151 automated tests and degrades to a rule-based analysis with explicit disclosure when generation is unavailable; of ten integration defects identified, six were repaired and four are documented as open. A quantum machine learning study conducted in two independent frameworks is reported alongside: the quantum kernel reproduces the classical result exactly at four orders of magnitude greater cost, and an analytical derivation shows why the chosen encoding determined that outcome in advance.

The International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision (ICD-11), is the World Health Organization's global standard for coding diseases and health-related conditions. Its entry QD85 defines burnout as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, characterised by exhaustion, increased mental distance from or cynicism towards one's job, and reduced professional efficacy [1]. The entry places burnout among factors influencing health status rather than among diseases, and that boundary binds any automated system built on it: such a system may report occupational risk, but it may not issue a diagnosis. Workplace communication, meanwhile, now leaves a continuous digital trace in which these signals are expressed daily, far more often than any survey can sample.

The instrument used in practice is the Maslach Burnout Inventory, which is reliable but administered periodically, dependent on self-report, and silent on why a particular score was produced [2]. Machine learning widens coverage, with ensemble models reaching an R² of 0.9567 by weighting workload, fatigue and tenure [3], but their explanations hold at the level of the population rather than of the individual a manager must actually speak to.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines parametric knowledge held in model weights with non-parametric knowledge retrieved from an external index at inference time, and was shown to improve performance and provenance on knowledge-intensive tasks [9]. Dense passage retrieval established that learned dual encoders outperform sparse lexical baselines such as the probabilistic relevance framework underlying BM25 [10], [11]. Efficient similarity search over the resulting vectors is supported by hierarchical navigable small world graphs [12] and by GPU-accelerated billion-scale indexing [13]. Sentence-BERT provides the sentence-level encoder family used here, deriving semantically meaningful fixed-length embeddings from siamese and triplet networks that can be compared by cosine similarity, reducing the cost of exhaustive pairwise comparison from hours to seconds [14].

To the knowledge of the authors, prior work treats burnout detection and burnout explanation as a single modelling problem. The contribution of this system is architectural: it treats them as two problems with different correctness criteria, joined by a contract that prevents the more fluent component from overruling the more accountable one.
